title: First use
question: What does someone have to give before they reach what they came for?
lede: When two disciples began to follow Jesus, he asked, “What do you want?”, and when they asked where he was staying, he said, “Come and see” (John 1:38–39). The first minutes in a faith app ask the same question from the other side. Many apps put a tour, an account, questions, a rating, permission prompts and a subscription offer in front of the first verse, prayer or answer. Some people arrive curious, some in a hard night, some coming back after years away or after being hurt in a church. Apps also cost money to build and run, and every AI answer has a price, so how and when to ask for support is a real question, not a trick. Welcome people first, and ask honestly.
calling: Welcome people as guests: let them reach what they came for first, keep help within reach, and ask for support honestly.

spectrum.title: From nothing asked to everything asked

working_example.situation: Someone has just installed a faith app. Choose what kind of app it is: a Bible reader, a prayer app or an AI companion. Then choose who is arriving: someone curious, someone in a hard night, or someone coming back after years away or after being hurt in a church. Count what each option asks before they reach what they came for, and see where help is. For the last option, compare asking for payment up front with asking after a first use.

options.name: Open on what they came for
options.origin: Familiar from church practice: the Diocese of York tells someone who has picked up a Bible to start with Mark, “Start with chapter 1 and read as much as feels manageable”; a pew Bible or a prayer book asks nothing first. The app, its passage, prayer and question box are written for this example.
options.gain: What they came for, at once
options.makes_easier: Nothing stands between the person and what they came for.
options.costs: Nothing is saved until they choose to save it.
options.ask_your_team: What is the one thing a new person should be able to do in the first ten seconds?

options.name: A first page of places to start
options.origin: Familiar from the Gideon Bible, whose front pages carry “topical indexes to point the reader to what the Bible says about various topics, problems and life situations”. Not observed in this form in an app. The situations, passages and help line are chosen for this example; the TelefonSeelsorge numbers are from its own website, checked 11 October 2026.
options.gain: A way in without a reference
options.makes_easier: A way in for someone without a reference, with help at the top.
options.costs: Someone chose the passages, and the list can feel like a diagnosis.
options.ask_your_team: Who chose these situations and passages, and what comes first for someone in danger?

options.name: Guest first, an account when there is something to keep
options.origin: Observed in Startblock (“Ohne Anmeldung fortfahren”, continue without signing in), Bible.is (“Create account later”) and Joseph Prince, where a guest can read and copy but is asked to sign up “to begin highlighting”; see the screenshots below. Apple’s review guidelines ask apps without significant account-based features to “let people use it without a login”. The wording here is written for this example.
options.cost: The later ask can feel like a wall
options.makes_easier: People use the app first and decide later whether to stay.
options.costs: The later ask can still feel like a wall, if it comes at the wrong moment.
options.ask_your_team: What is the first thing worth keeping, and is that the right moment to ask?

options.name: A short tour first
options.origin: Observed in Startblock’s five skippable intro slides, whose fourth reads “Das brauchst du: Eine Bibel aus Papier, ein Notizheft, einen Stift und etwas Zeit” (you need a paper Bible, a notebook, a pen and some time), in ESV’s welcome carousel, which ends in an offer to create a free account, and in Joseph Prince’s intro video and feature tour; see the screenshots below. The slides here are written for this example.
options.makes_easier: Sets expectations, as Startblock’s paper Bible and pen do.
options.costs: Often skipped and soon forgotten; it delays the first use.
options.ask_your_team: What would a person miss if they skipped every slide?

options.name: Questions first
options.origin: Observed in Abide’s “What brings you here today?” photo grid, Bible BFF’s “How much of the Bible have you read?” and Faith’s questions for a name, an age range and a profile picture; see the screenshots below and the check-ins deep dive. The questions here are written for this example.
options.costs: Every question delays the first use, and some ask what is not needed.
options.ask_your_team: What does each answer change, and can someone skip it?

options.name: Asking for payment
options.origin: Observed in Bible BFF, which asks people to rate the app before using it and then offers a weekly plan; Spark Bible, which asks for notifications before the first verse and later says “You just used your last free study”; Abide, whose trial screen gives the reminder day and charge date; and Pray.com, which asks for a mobile number at sign-up; see the screenshots below. The second setting, asking after a first use and saying what things cost, is a proposal; its costs are our estimate from published AI prices.
options.cost: Up front, it asks before giving
options.makes_easier: Asked after a first use, honestly, it keeps the work going.
options.costs: Asked before anything is given, it turns people away and puts help behind a wall.
options.ask_your_team: What is free, what costs you money, and does the person know before they pay?

takeaways.heading: Let people reach what they came for first
takeaways.text: Startblock offers “Ohne Anmeldung fortfahren” (continue without signing in), and Bible.is “Create account later”. Open on today’s passage, a prayer to play or a question box, and count everything asked before it.

takeaways.heading: Ask for an account when there is something to keep
takeaways.text: Joseph Prince lets a guest read and copy, and asks for an account “to begin highlighting”. A highlight, a plan or a conversation worth keeping is the honest moment to ask; say what the account holds, and how to delete it.

takeaways.heading: Ask for permissions when a feature needs them
takeaways.text: Spark Bible asks for notifications before the first verse; Android’s guidance is to ask “in context, when the user starts to interact with the feature that requires it”. Ask when someone sets a reminder.

takeaways.heading: Help in a crisis comes before everything
takeaways.text: Someone may open a faith app in a hard night. Keep a way to a person on the first screen, and never put it behind an account, a question, a free-answer limit or a paywall. Offer help, not verses, unless the person asks for Scripture.

takeaways.heading: “No church right now” is an ordinary answer
takeaways.text: Someone coming back after years away, or after being hurt in a church, may meet questions about their church on the first screen. Ask only if the answer changes something, let it be skipped, and don’t praise or correct any answer.

takeaways.heading: Ask for payment after a first use, and say what costs money
takeaways.text: Abide’s trial screen gives the reminder day and the charge date; Spark Bible tells people when they have used their “last free study”. Say what is free, what costs money and roughly why: licensed notes, recordings, AI answers. A free allowance that explains itself is fairer than a wall.

takeaways.heading: Neither free nor paid is the only faithful way
takeaways.text: The church has long supported those who serve the word, and has long distrusted those who sell it. A subscription can be honest and a free app can be manipulative. The test is what is asked before anything is given, and whether the person knows what they are paying for.

findings.heading: Come and see
findings.text: Jesus asked two would-be followers, “What do you want?”, and answered their question with an invitation: “Come and see” (John 1:38–39). They spent the rest of the day with him.

findings.heading: Guests received like Christ
findings.text: The Rule of Benedict asks that “all guests who arrive be received like Christ”, and, for someone asking to join the community, that they “not be granted an easy entrance”. Welcome is free; commitment is asked for later, of those who want to stay.

findings.heading: A place to start, and permission to read a little
findings.text: The Diocese of York tells someone who has picked up a Bible to try Mark: “Start with chapter 1 and read as much as feels manageable. You could also listen to it.” The Gideons put “topical indexes” for “topics, problems and life situations” at the front of their Bibles.

research.subtitle: Paying those who serve the word

findings.heading: The worker is worthy of his wages
findings.text: The Levites received the tithes of Israel “in return for the work they do” (Numbers 18:21). Paul wrote that “those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel” (1 Corinthians 9:14) and that “the one who receives instruction in the word must share in all good things with his instructor” (Galatians 6:6). He also chose, for himself, to “offer it free of charge” (1 Corinthians 9:18).

findings.heading: Offerings, and a line against trading
findings.text: Catholic church law permits a priest “to receive an offering to apply the Mass for a specific intention”, by which the faithful “support its ministers and works”, and requires that “Any appearance of … trading is to be excluded entirely”. Protestant churches pay their ministers through offerings, tithes or, in Germany, church tax.

findings.heading: Support, and suspicion of those who ask
findings.text: The Didache, an early church manual, says a true teacher “is himself worthy, as the workman, of his support”, and that a travelling apostle who asks for money “is a false prophet”. Peter told Simon, who offered money for the Spirit, “you thought you could buy the gift of God with money!” (Acts 8:20), and Paul refused to “peddle the word of God for profit” (2 Corinthians 2:17).

research.subtitle: What a first use asks, and what it costs

findings.heading: Use first, then decide
findings.text: Apple’s review guidelines say that an app without significant account-based features should “let people use it without a login”, and that an app with accounts must let people delete them. Its design guidance asks for onboarding that is “fast, fun, and optional”, and for letting people experience an app “before prompting them for ratings or purchases”.

findings.heading: Tutorials are skipped
findings.text: Nielsen Norman Group found that deck-of-cards tutorials “didn’t improve task performance”, and that users “frequently skip them”.

findings.heading: A required account turns people away
findings.text: In Baymard’s survey of US online shoppers, 18% of those who abandoned a checkout for reasons other than browsing said “The site wanted me to create an account”. That is shopping, not faith apps, but the moment is the same: someone ready to begin is asked for something first.

findings.heading: Asking again and again
findings.text: European data protection authorities name “continuous prompting” a deceptive design pattern: users “repeatedly asked” for more data or consent tend to give in.

findings.heading: What it costs to serve someone
findings.text: An AI answer that reads about 6,000 tokens (instructions, passages and the conversation so far) and writes about 600 costs about 1.8 cents on Claude Sonnet 5.5 and about a tenth of a cent on Claude Haiku 5.5, at published prices. At 20 answers a day, that is about $10.80 or $0.54 a person each month, before hosting and staff. Translations cost too: Crossway’s free ESV terms exclude apps that sell, take donations or carry advertising, while the Berean Standard Bible is in the public domain. And free apps are paid for by someone: in 2018 YouVersion’s $8.3 million budget came from a church’s tithes and donations.

which_fits.start_with: Open on today’s passage; ask for an account when someone wants to keep something
Play first; ask for notifications when someone sets a reminder
A free allowance that says why, with crisis help never counted
A price after a first use, with the trial’s reminder and charge dates

which_fits.if: You are tempted to put the paywall first
which_fits.start_with: Don’t: let people meet what you made, then ask, honestly

pulls_against.title: Saying whose teaching it is, and welcoming the sceptic
options_here: Open on what they came for
Guest first, an account when there is something to keep
pulls_against.pull: Honesty means naming a church at the door, but a church label or a step that asks people to choose a tradition can feel like a membership test to an enquirer or to someone a church has hurt.
pulls_against.hold: Say whose teaching the assistant follows in one plain line, as a description rather than a gate. Never make someone choose a church before they may ask a question.

pulls_against.title: Paying for answers, and limits that serve the person
pulls_against.pull: Every AI answer has a real cost, and a message allowance can look just like a limit that sells more conversations.
pulls_against.hold: An allowance is a price, so call it one. Keep it apart from limits that protect rest, never let it end a hard conversation, and never count crisis help against it.

pulls_against.title: Asking nothing at the door, and knowing a child might be there
options_here: Guest first, an account when there is something to keep
Open on what they came for
pulls_against.pull: A first use that asks for nothing leaves a team unable to tell when a child has reached the chat.
pulls_against.hold: Design the chat as if a child might be on the other side. Keep open chat out of guest mode, or make guest chat safe for children by default, rather than relying on a typed age.

reflection.heading: What a welcome is for
reflection.text: Jesus asked two would-be followers, “What do you want?”, and answered with an invitation: “Come and see” (John 1:38–39). Isaiah’s call is to “come, buy wine and milk without money and without cost!” (Isaiah 55:1), and the last page of the Bible invites “the one who desires the water of life” to “drink freely” (Revelation 22:17). Grace is not for sale, and a first welcome should feel like it.

reflection.heading: Where Christians differ, and agree
reflection.text: The same Scriptures pay those who serve: the Levites lived from the tithe (Numbers 18:21), and “the worker is worthy of his wages” (Luke 10:7). Catholics give an offering for a Mass, under canon law that excludes “any appearance of … trading”; Protestant churches pay ministers from offerings, tithes or church tax; Paul took support from some churches and chose to preach to others “free of charge” (1 Corinthians 9:18). Both traditions warn against those who “peddle the word of God for profit” (2 Corinthians 2:17). An app that charges is in a long line of honest support, and of temptation.

reflection.heading: What follows for design
reflection.text: Let people come and see before anything is asked of them. Keep help within reach from the first screen. Then ask for support as the church at its best has done: openly, for real costs, never for access to grace, and never from someone in a crisis. Say what is free, what costs money and why, and let people pay what they can.

voices.note: told Methodists to “gain all you can” by honest work, but called gain made “by hurting our neighbour in his soul” “dear-bought”; then to save all you can and “give all you can”.

three_ways.exploitative: Put a quiz, a rating, permission prompts and a weekly trial before the first verse; make the free tier feel like a punishment; keep crisis help behind the paywall.
three_ways.ethical: Open on what people came for, ask for an account when there is something to keep, ask for payment after a first use, and give the trial’s reminder and charge dates.
three_ways.redemptive: Keep Scripture and crisis help free, say plainly what things cost you, let people pay what they can, and give up the conversions that a gate before the first use would bring.

decide.question: What must someone give before they reach what they came for, and what does it honestly cost you to serve them?
decide.exercise: Install your app on a fresh phone and write down every screen, field, prompt and offer before the first verse, prayer or answer. Do it again as someone who types, in the first box they see, that they don’t want to be here anymore. Then write one paragraph, in plain words, telling a new user what is free, what costs money, roughly what it costs you, and why. Would you be glad for them to read it on the first day?

examples.title: “Pray for others, be prayed for”
examples.observed: Captured 19 September 2025 · from embedded image metadata
examples.observation: The Community tab, signed out, shows a small church on a purple background and “Sign in or create an account to pray alongside your community”, with three ticks: “Connect with your parish community and stay connected with fellow members”, “Pray for others, be prayed for” and “Strengthen your faith together through community challenges and discussions”.
examples.decision: The pitch makes the parish the audience. Hallow’s help centre adds the details that matter: requests of up to 240 characters, never anonymous, active for seven days, answered with a heart.
examples.limits: A still image shows one interface state. Gestures, timing, accessibility, persistence and what happens next were not tested. App version not recorded.

examples.title: “What brings you here today?” as a photo grid
examples.observed: Captured 17 October 2025 · from embedded image metadata
examples.observation: A multi-select grid of twelve photo tiles (Reduce Anxiety, Grow Spiritually, Feel Peace, Sleep Better, Strengthen Relationships, Connect With God, Trust God, Experience Freedom, Increase Hope, Receive Healing, Improve Character, Love Well) under “Select one or more to continue.” Earlier steps ask for content types; between steps, interstitials show listener counts and five-star testimonials before a subscription offer.
examples.decision: Goals can shape a first suggestion. Say what each choice changes, let people skip, and keep social proof and sales out of the questions themselves.

sources.title: App Store Review Guidelines
sources.author: Apple
sources.shows: “If your app doesn’t include significant account-based features, let people use it without a login. If your app supports account creation, you must also offer account deletion within the app.” Apps “may not require users to enter personal information to function, except when directly relevant to the core functionality of the app or required by law.”
sources.application: Let people read, pray or ask before they sign up, and let them delete the account they make.
sources.limits: Platform rules for the App Store; enforcement varies, and Google Play has its own rules.

sources.title: Human Interface Guidelines: Onboarding
sources.author: Apple
sources.shows: Onboarding should be “fast, fun, and optional”; “Postpone nonessential setup flows or customization steps”; “Prefer letting people experience your app or game before prompting them for ratings or purchases.”
sources.application: Open on the content; ask for ratings and payment after people have used the app.

sources.title: Request runtime permissions
sources.author: Android Developers
sources.shows: “Ask for a permission in context, when the user starts to interact with the feature that requires it. Don’t block the user.”
sources.application: Ask for notifications when someone sets a reminder, not at launch.
sources.limits: Platform guidance for Android; Apple’s is similar.

sources.title: Mobile-App Onboarding: An Analysis of Components and Techniques
sources.author: Alita Kendrick · Nielsen Norman Group · 21 June 2020
sources.shows: “Skip Onboarding Whenever Possible”; their research on deck-of-cards tutorials “showed that tutorials didn’t improve task performance”; “lengthy promotional onboarding will likely be skipped.”
sources.application: Spend the effort on a clear first screen rather than slides about it.
sources.limits: An expert article drawing on the group’s own studies; details of those studies are in separate reports.

sources.title: Onboarding Tutorials vs. Contextual Help
sources.author: Nielsen Norman Group
sources.shows: Tutorials are “dramatically overused”, and “we find that users frequently skip them”; “Users want to start using the product right away.”
sources.application: Teach a feature when someone reaches it, not before the first use.
sources.limits: An expert article; the group notes tutorials can help with genuinely new interactions.

sources.title: Guidelines 03/2022 on deceptive design patterns in social media platform interfaces
sources.author: European Data Protection Board · version 2.0, 14 February 2023
sources.shows: “Continuous prompting” occurs “when users are pushed to provide more personal data than necessary for the purposes of processing or to agree with another use of their data, by being repeatedly asked”; at sign-up, users “should understand what exactly they sign up for”.
sources.application: Ask once, for what is needed, and say plainly what someone is signing up for.
sources.limits: Written for social media platforms; it applies the GDPR, which binds other apps too.

sources.title: Cart abandonment rate statistics
sources.author: Baymard Institute
sources.shows: Among US online shoppers who abandoned a checkout for reasons other than “just browsing”, 18% gave the reason “The site wanted me to create an account”.
sources.application: A required account turns some people away at the moment they were ready.
sources.limits: Online shopping, not faith apps; a survey of stated reasons.

sources.title: Start with the Bible
sources.author: Diocese of York (Church of England)
sources.shows: For someone who has “Picked up a Bible and wondering where to begin”: try Mark; “Start with chapter 1 and read as much as feels manageable. You could also listen to it.” It suggests a short prayer before beginning.
sources.application: A church’s first step asks nothing of the reader: a place to start, and permission to read only a little.

sources.title: Help from the Bible
sources.author: The Gideons International in Australia
sources.shows: “The front section of all Gideon Bibles and Testaments contains Helps to read the Bible. There are a number of topical indexes to point the reader to what the Bible says about various topics, problems and life situations.”
sources.application: A first page of situations is an old way into Scripture for someone without a reference.
sources.limits: One national association’s description; editions differ.

sources.title: St. Benedict’s Rule for Monasteries
sources.author: Benedict of Nursia, sixth century · Project Gutenberg edition
sources.shows: Chapter 53: “Let all guests who arrive be received like Christ.” Chapter 58, on someone asking to join the community: “let him not be granted an easy entrance”.
sources.application: Welcome guests freely; ask for commitment later, from those who want to stay.
sources.limits: A monastic rule; an app is not a monastery, and the analogy is ours.

sources.title: Code of Canon Law, canons 879–958: the Most Holy Eucharist
sources.author: Holy See
sources.shows: A priest “is permitted to receive an offering to apply the Mass for a specific intention” (can. 945); those who give it “share its concern to support its ministers and works” (can. 946); and “Any appearance of … trading is to be excluded entirely from the offering for Masses” (can. 947).
sources.application: The church has long let people give for the ministry of the word and sacrament, and drawn a line against trading in it.
sources.limits: Catholic church law; Protestant churches support ministry through offerings, church tax or tithes.

sources.title: The Didache (Teaching of the Twelve Apostles)
sources.author: Early Christian text, late first or early second century · New Advent edition
sources.shows: A travelling apostle should “take nothing but bread … but if he ask money, he is a false prophet”; yet “every true prophet that wills to abide among you is worthy of his support. So also a true teacher is himself worthy, as the workman, of his support.”
sources.application: The early church supported its teachers and distrusted those who asked for money: both at once.
sources.limits: An early church manual; its dating and setting are debated.

sources.title: Pricing
sources.author: Anthropic
sources.shows: Claude Sonnet 5.5 costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens; Claude Haiku 5.5 costs $0.10 and $0.50 for prompts up to 100,000 tokens.
sources.application: Every AI answer has a cost; the choice of model changes it many times over.
sources.limits: One provider’s list prices in US dollars; prices change, and other providers differ.

sources.title: ESV API: introduction
sources.author: Crossway
sources.shows: The text is free “for non-commercial use”; a commercial site “is primarily designed to motivate visitors to buy something, to pay for a service, or to give a donation, or it accepts advertising or sponsorships”. Other uses need permission.
sources.application: The translation an app uses can decide whether it may charge or ask for donations at all.
sources.limits: One publisher’s terms; others differ, and the Berean Standard Bible is in the public domain.

sources.title: Berean Bible terms and conditions
sources.author: Berean Bible
sources.shows: The Berean Standard Bible was dedicated to the public domain on 30 April 2023.
sources.application: Public-domain modern translations can be compared, quoted and shared without licence limits.

sources.title: With 330 million downloads, top Bible app celebrates 10 years
sources.author: Religion News Service · Word&Way, 27 July 2018
sources.shows: “An $8.3 million annual budget, funded by Life Church members’ tithes and outside donations, pays for YouVersion”; the app is “free with no commercial advertisements”.
sources.application: A free app is still paid for, here by a church and its donors.
sources.limits: A 2018 report; the current budget is not public in this source.

sources.title: TelefonSeelsorge
sources.author: TelefonSeelsorge Deutschland (Protestant and Catholic churches)
sources.shows: “Tag und Nacht erreichbar 0800 1110111 / 0800 1110222 oder 116 123”, by phone, chat or email.
sources.application: A first screen can carry a way to a person, day and night, free of charge.
sources.limits: Germany; other countries have their own services.

review.what: Help for someone arriving in a hard night, the wording for someone coming back after being hurt in a church, and the reflection on paying for Scripture, teaching and AI
